artworks.title: The Harriet Beecher Stowe House
artworks.description: A brick “Gothic cottage”, painted grey, built in 1871 as a speculative house. Stowe bought it in 1873 and lived here with her husband Calvin and their twin daughters for the last 23 years of her life; she died here in 1896. Her grand-niece Katharine Seymour Day saved it, and it opened as a museum in 1968, one of the first house museums about a woman. A National Historic Landmark, restored in 2016–17 with wallpapers and carpets based on Stowe’s own choices.
artworks.galleryName: Harriet Beecher Stowe House (1871): Stowe’s home from 1873 to 1896, seen on guided tours only. Pick floor 1 or 2 above to see its rooms

artworks.title: The Visitor Center
artworks.description: Once the carriage house, now the first stop: buy tickets here for the Stowe House Experience, look around the museum store (New Dawn Bookstore by River Bend Bookshop) and use the accessible restroom. Every tour starts here.
artworks.galleryName: Visitor Center (1873, once a carriage house): start here for tickets, the museum store and the restroom. Pick floor V above
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: The Katharine Seymour Day House
artworks.description: A Queen Anne mansion of rough pink granite, brick and carved wood, built for Franklin and Mary Chamberlin. Stowe’s grand-niece Katharine Seymour Day (1870–1964), who founded the Stowe Center in 1941, bought it that year to save it from demolition. It holds the research library, offices and collection storage, and opens only for some exhibits and programs. Its outside paint, shingles and finials were restored to their 1884 look.
artworks.galleryName: Katharine Seymour Day House (1884): research library (by appointment) and offices; open only for some exhibits, programs and tours
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: The Research Library
artworks.description: More than 12,000 books, 4,000 pamphlets, 180,000 manuscripts and 12,000 images about Stowe, the Beecher family, Nook Farm and Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Open by appointment only (860-522-9258 ext. 313).
artworks.galleryName: Katharine Seymour Day House (1884): research library (by appointment) and offices; open only for some exhibits, programs and tours
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: Stowe’s gardens
artworks.description: Stowe loved gardening and wrote about it. The beds are planted informally with the flowers she wrote about: sweet peas, peonies, foxglove, bee balm, nasturtium, daylilies, marigolds, asters and goldenrod, so something is in bloom from April to September. Look for grafts of the pink Stowe Dogwood and the award-winning heritage roses.
artworks.galleryName: Wildflower Garden, just south of the Stowe House: peonies, lilac, old roses and “Uncle Tom” tulips (place approximate)
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: “Uncle Tom” tulips
artworks.description: In late April and early May the south garden next to the house fills with deep red double tulips named “Uncle Tom”, a Dutch variety of 1939. Nobody knows how they got the name.
artworks.galleryName: Wildflower Garden, just south of the Stowe House: peonies, lilac, old roses and “Uncle Tom” tulips (place approximate)
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: Harriet Beecher Stowe, reading
artworks.description: A life-size bronze of Stowe, beautifully dressed and seated on a bench, reading the 1849 freedom narrative of Josiah Henson, the man who inspired her Uncle Tom. Sit down beside her. Gift of Rosamond Warren Allen.
artworks.galleryName: The new shade garden in the centre of the campus, behind the Stowe House, by Connecticut’s largest Star Magnolia, with the bronze statue of Stowe (place approximate)

artworks.title: Connecticut’s largest Star Magnolia
artworks.description: The state’s biggest Star Magnolia stands at the centre of the campus. In 2026 a new shade garden was planted around it: dogwood, cornelian cherry, more than 125 shrubs, 130 ferns and 375 perennials, most native to New England.

artworks.title: The Merrill Magnolia and the Sensory Garden
artworks.description: The state-champion Merrill Magnolia towers over the west side of the house and blooms in May. Its limbs root where they touch the ground. A deep wind chime hangs in it above the Sensory Garden and its bird bath.

artworks.title: Little Free Library and Pantry
artworks.description: Built by the Stowe Center’s facilities manager and painted by Isys B., an Asylum Hill student: take a book or some food, or leave some for a neighbour.
artworks.galleryName: Little Free Library and Pantry, in front of the Day House: take a book, leave a book

artworks.title: The Nook Farm neighbourhood
artworks.description: Nook Farm was home to writers, reformers and activists: Stowe, Mark Twain, her sister the suffragist Isabella Beecher Hooker, the writer Charles Dudley Warner and the actor William Gillette. The Twain House is next door; a self-guided audio tour of the neighbourhood costs $15.
artworks.galleryName: Stowe Center campus: 2.5 acres of historic and new gardens, open for picnics (boundary approximate)
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: The entrance hall and its Madonnas
artworks.description: Walking in, notice how many pictures of the Madonna hang in the house; Stowe painted some of them herself.

artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: The front parlor
artworks.description: Stowe’s salon, where tours now sit down to talk about the issues she wrote about. The photo shows Stowe in her parlor in 1886; the Stowe Center used it, and visitors’ letters, to remake the room’s fancy black wallpaper border and its colours in 2017. The 1960s restoration had treated the two parlors as one room.
artworks.galleryName: Front parlor, with its bay window: Stowe’s “salon”, where tours sit down to talk
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: $2,500 Reward!
artworks.description: A reward poster for people who escaped slavery: one of the documents tours read closely together in the front parlor.

artworks.description: A bronze statuette awarded to Stowe by the managers of the Boston Anti-Slavery Fair in 1853. Stowe filled her parlors with gifts and souvenirs from her travels.

artworks.title: Florida Orange Fruit & Blossoms
artworks.description: Stowe painted all her life. This oil on panel shows oranges from Mandarin, Florida, where the family spent their winters; she gave some of her paintings to raise money for schools and churches for freed people in Florida.

artworks.title: The back parlor
artworks.description: The second parlor, now decorated as its own room, with copies of old masters such as Raphael and Giorgione and souvenirs from Stowe’s travels. Where photos of this house were missing, the finishes follow her first Hartford house, Oakholm: the picture shows Oakholm’s double parlor about 1865.

artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: Spill vase: Eliza crossing the ice
artworks.description: A porcelain vase painted to order with Eliza and her son Harry running across the frozen Ohio River to freedom: the most famous scene of Uncle Tom’s Cabin.
artworks.galleryName: Back parlor
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: The dining room
artworks.description: Set for a family meal. Its wallpaper is a reproduction of a paper kept in the Stowe Center’s archive, hung by Denis Picard of Kensington, CT, in 2017 (the photo).

artworks.title: The table where Stowe began Uncle Tom’s Cabin
artworks.description: A drop-leaf table, a wedding present from Stowe’s father. She wrote the first two chapters of Uncle Tom’s Cabin on it, in Brunswick, Maine, in 1851. Today passages of the book are projected on a screen behind it.
artworks.galleryName: Dining room
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: Calvin Stowe
artworks.description: Harriet’s husband, a professor of the Bible whom she described as “rich in Greek & Hebrew, Latin & Arabic, & alas! rich in nothing else”. His study is now a multimedia room.
artworks.galleryName: Calvin Stowe’s study, now a multimedia room
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: The kitchen
artworks.description: The last room of the tour, set up as in Stowe’s day with a coal stove at one end and a big table in the middle. Stowe employed African American, Irish and German women here. Visitors sit at the table and write their own thoughts on the paper that covers it.
artworks.galleryName: Kitchen: the last room of the tour
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Stowe Center’s own pages.

artworks.title: Stowe’s bedroom
artworks.description: Harriet Beecher Stowe’s bedroom. You can rent it for an hour or two as “Harriet’s Writing Room” and write there (Mondays and Tuesdays, $300 an hour).
artworks.galleryName: Harriet Beecher Stowe’s bedroom (rented out as “Harriet’s Writing Room”)

artworks.title: The Stowe Gallery for Hope & Freedom
artworks.description: The former “Global Impact of Uncle Tom’s Cabin” room, reinterpreted. It starts with Stowe’s 1853 Key to Uncle Tom’s Cabin and centres the Black writers who influenced her, from freedom narratives to Stowe Prize winners Ta-Nehisi Coates, Ruha Benjamin and Bettina Love. Seen on the 60-minute Inspiring Stowe tour.
artworks.galleryName: The Stowe Gallery for Hope & Freedom
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: What Does It Mean to Be Human?
artworks.description: Current exhibition: intimate works by the artist and muralist Amanda Mendoza, with research by Gamze Ozker, on how humanity is denied and reclaimed, from slavery to today’s immigrants, using hands and nature as symbols.
artworks.galleryName: Gallery for Literary Activism: changing exhibitions
artworks.placeNote: Shown by the Stowe Center; the room it is in is our guess (no plan is published).

artworks.title: Uncle Tom’s Cabin, first edition
artworks.description: The novel came out week by week in The National Era in 1851–52 and as a book in March 1852; it sold 300,000 copies in its first year in the U.S. The Stowe Center has most American and foreign editions.

artworks.title: Gold “slave bracelet”
artworks.description: Given to Stowe on her 1853 tour of Britain: a gold bracelet shaped like a slave’s shackle, with links engraved with dates of abolition. Stowe later had the date of American emancipation added.
